newsitem.title: USA: U.S. FDA panel opposes new female contraceptive.
newsitem.headline: U.S. FDA panel opposes new female contraceptive.

text.p: A federal advisory committee on Monday recommended against Food and Drug Administration approval of a new one-size-fits-all vaginal barrier contraceptive device.

The FDA's Obstetrics and Gynecology Devices Panel, following a day-long hearing, said there was insufficient trial data to show the vaginal barrier device, called "Lea's Shield," was effective in preventing pregnancies.
YAMA Inc., of Millburn, N.J., the device's maker, wanted approval to market the shield by prescription.
Panel review is the first step toward agency approval of a new drug or medical device. The FDA is not bound to follow the recommendations of the panels, but usually accepts them.
The panel voted 7-1 against a favorable recommendation.
It said the size of the trial -- 52 couples -- was not adequate to show the device's effectiveness.
YAMA had said that, unlike such devices as the diaphragm and cervical cap now on the market, its shield fitted most women and did not require sizing and fitting by a doctor.
The device, which would be be used with a spermicidal cream or gel, was seen by women's advocay groups as another choice a woman could make on her own to prevent pregnancy.
Some FDA officials were concerned, however, that women might believe the device was useful to prevent sexually transmitted diseases (STD).
They added that no tests have shown the shield can protect against a STD and no such claims were being made.
The shield is already on the market for over-the-counter sale in continential Europe and in Canada, YAMA said.
